title: Commanders of Attention 2: The Magnetizers
hook: The blank field on the hawk card keeps every volunteer watching the carrier.
counterintuition: Held attention is not the same as suspense. A magnetizer works when self-relevance, unfinished information, or mystery keeps the mind with a question the message can truly answer.
tryThisNow: Take one ignored request and turn it into a real unanswered question. Name what is unfinished, personal, or unknown, then answer it directly.
keyTakeaway: Magnetizers hold attention by opening a real loop that the next message can close, not by teasing for its own sake.

breakdown.fastRead:
A wildlife intake card sits beside a taped carrier. Every field is filled except one: last food seen. The blank space keeps volunteers looking at the hawk because treatment depends on the missing answer.

Some cues hold the mind in place. A cue can feel personal, leave a task open, or pose a real question. It works only when the next message closes that loop. The cheap version spends curiosity on an unrelated ask.
breakdown.deepRead:
An insurance renewal letter starts with the customer’s own street and a flood-zone map. The premium table comes later. The street name keeps the homeowner reading because the information is about their house, not about insurance in general.

Self-relevance has gravity.

Frozen support names self-relevant, unfinished, and mysterious cues as magnetizers. They do not merely seize attention for a second. They hold it long enough for association and persuasion to build. That staying power is useful only when the held question belongs to the choice.

A studio mentor covers the final rendering and leaves one unresolved stair section visible. Students lean in because the gap asks to be closed. A trainer clips three anonymous receipts to a cork strip and asks which visit lost the shopper. The reveal matters because the greeting note actually answers the mystery.
breakdown.fullRead:
The strongest magnetizers do not yell. They tug. A street name in the first line of a renewal letter. An empty timestamp slot on a courtroom timeline. A single unchecked export box on a cancellation screen. Each one keeps attention because the mind wants completion, personal relevance, or an answer.

That pull can be clean. A homeowner deserves to know that the flood-zone change affects their own address before scanning premium options. A volunteer deserves to see which missing intake fact blocks treatment. Jurors deserve to mark the unexplained gap before the final timestamp appears. In each case, the open loop improves judgment.

What would make the open loop unfair?

A false progress bar on a cancellation screen is not an honest magnetizer. It holds attention by implying the user has unfinished setup when the only real task is an optional data export. Once the designer removes the false bar and keeps the export checkbox, attention stays with something legitimate. The user can finish or leave with eyes open.

Mystery needs an answer. Unfinished information needs a consequence. Self-relevance needs a real link to the person in front of you. If any of those are missing, the cue becomes a hook with no responsibility behind it.

Leave people with a question only when you are prepared to answer it.

examples.title: Olivia Starts With Maple Street

planSpec.audience: a policy designer trying to keep homeowners reading
planSpec.stakes: whether self-relevance holds attention past the first paragraph
planSpec.requiredBeat: the designer opens with the customer’s street flood-zone change, then reveals the premium options

examples.scenario: A renewal letter begins with Maple Street in the first line, and Olivia keeps the flood-zone map above the premium table. Before the redesign, homeowners skimmed past the general risk paragraph. After the street name appears first, they read to the options. Olivia must decide whether personalization is justified only where the map actually changes the customer’s home risk.
examples.whatToDo: Open with the customer’s street flood-zone change, then show the premium table. Use self-relevance only where the policy data truly applies.
examples.whyItMatters: A real address holds attention because it changes the homeowner’s own decision. Generic personalization would look similar but carry less truth.

examples.title: Anders Leaves the Stair Section Unresolved

planSpec.audience: a studio mentor keeping students engaged with unfinished designs
planSpec.stakes: whether an unresolved edge holds attention better than a completed rendering
planSpec.requiredBeat: the mentor covers the final rendering and leaves the unresolved stair section visible while students predict the fix

examples.scenario: A half-pinned floor plan curls at one corner while a vellum overlay hides the final rendering. Anders leaves the stair section visible and asks students to predict the fix before the critique moves on. The room keeps looking at the gap. He is thinking about how much longer attention stays when the design is unfinished in exactly the place where judgment has to happen.
examples.whatToDo: Cover the final rendering and leave the stair problem open. Ask for predictions before revealing the completed design.
examples.whyItMatters: The unfinished stair holds attention because it asks for completion. Students stay with the problem instead of admiring a finished image.

examples.title: Megan Reveals the Greeting Note Last

planSpec.audience: a retail trainer teaching associates to notice greeting gaps
planSpec.stakes: whether a mystery queue keeps attention through a dull protocol
planSpec.requiredBeat: the trainer shows three anonymous receipts and asks which visit lost the shopper before revealing the greeting note

examples.scenario: Three anonymous receipts are clipped to a cork strip as Megan begins a dull protocol refresher. At 9:05 a.m. in the training room, Megan is the service trainer deciding how long the receipt mystery should stay open. Each receipt has a time stamp, return total, and no names. She asks associates which visit lost the shopper before revealing the greeting note. They must decide from the receipts first, then watch the missing hello explain the loss better than another training slide.
examples.whatToDo: Show the receipts, ask for predictions, then reveal the greeting note. Let the mystery close on the exact behavior the protocol requires.
examples.whyItMatters: The unknown keeps attention through routine material. The reveal works because it answers the question with a concrete greeting gap.

examples.title: Sam Leaves One Hawk Field Blank

planSpec.audience: a volunteer coordinator explaining why incomplete records matter
planSpec.stakes: whether unfinished information keeps volunteers tracking the animal past intake
planSpec.requiredBeat: the coordinator leaves one field blank on a rescued hawk card and asks what treatment becomes impossible

examples.scenario: A hawk intake card lies beside a taped carrier with the carrier label half peeled. At 4:25 p.m. in the wildlife intake room, Ingrid is the volunteer lead deciding which missing fact the next instruction must answer. Sam leaves the last-food-seen field blank while new volunteers reach for towels. He is about to decide whether to lecture about complete records or ask what treatment becomes impossible without that missing line. The blank field keeps every eye on the card and the bird inside the carrier.
examples.whatToDo: Leave the key field blank and ask what treatment decision cannot be made. Fill it only after volunteers name the consequence.
examples.whyItMatters: The unfinished card holds attention because the gap blocks care. Completion is not paperwork; it changes what the animal can receive.

examples.title: Diane Withholds the Final Timestamp

planSpec.audience: a trial consultant helping jurors follow a timeline
planSpec.stakes: whether mystery should be opened only where evidence can close it
planSpec.requiredBeat: the consultant withholds the final timestamp until jurors have marked the unexplained gap themselves

examples.scenario: A timeline board has one empty timestamp slot, and Diane keeps the final timestamp card inside an evidence binder. Jurors will have to decide whether the sequence makes sense. Before the exhibit order is locked, she asks the team to let jurors mark the unexplained gap themselves, then reveal the final card. She must decide whether the mystery is fair because the evidence can close it.
examples.whatToDo: Withhold the timestamp long enough for jurors to mark the gap, then reveal the evidence card. Do not open a mystery the record cannot answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The empty slot holds attention while preserving fairness. The question is legitimate because the evidence closes the loop.

examples.title: Paul Removes the False Progress Bar

planSpec.audience: a service designer trying to retain users ethically
planSpec.stakes: whether an unfinished setup checklist holds attention without trapping the user
planSpec.requiredBeat: the designer removes the false progress bar and keeps only the real unfinished data export task

examples.scenario: A cancellation screen shows one unchecked export box beside the cancel button. Paul’s postmortem starts with the false progress bar he removed after users said they felt trapped. The only unfinished task left is the real data export. He can see why attention still holds, but now it points to a choice users may actually want before leaving.
examples.whatToDo: Remove the false progress bar and keep only the real export checkbox near the cancel button. Let unfinished status reflect an actual user task.
examples.whyItMatters: Held attention becomes manipulative when the unfinished item is fake. The export box is legitimate because it names a real consequence of leaving.

questions.prompt: A renewal letter starts with a homeowner’s street and a flood-zone change before showing premium options. Why does this hold attention?
choices: The street name makes the risk self-relevant before the table appears.
The letter looks more formal than a generic renewal.
The premium table becomes less important.
questions.explanation: The address holds attention because it changes the homeowner’s own situation. Formality is secondary, and the premium table still matters after the personal risk is clear.

questions.prompt: An architecture mentor wants students to stay engaged with a stair design problem. Which move best uses an unfinished loop?
choices: Show the polished rendering first so everyone sees the answer.
Cover the final rendering and leave the unresolved stair section visible for predictions.
Ask students to vote on the prettiest drawing.
questions.explanation: The unresolved stair keeps attention on the problem the critique must solve. A finished rendering closes the loop too soon, and prettiness pulls attention away from the design issue.

questions.prompt: A retail trainer shows three receipts and asks which visit lost the shopper before revealing a missing greeting note. What makes this fair mystery?
choices: The reveal answers the exact question associates were asked to solve.
The receipts make the exercise feel like a game.
The trainer withholds all evidence until the end.
questions.explanation: The mystery is fair because the greeting note closes the open question. Game feel is not the point, and withholding all evidence would make prediction pointless.

questions.prompt: A volunteer coordinator leaves one intake field blank on a rescued hawk card. What should happen next? Inside the rescue intake room, she must decide whether the blank field will be answered by the next instruction or left as a tease.
choices: Fill it quickly so volunteers do not feel uncomfortable.
Ask which treatment decision becomes impossible without the missing field.
Ignore the blank and show photos of successful rescues.
questions.explanation: The blank field should hold attention on the consequence of incomplete records. Filling it too fast closes the loop, while rescue photos add emotion without teaching the intake need.

questions.prompt: A trial consultant wants jurors to notice a timeline gap. Which choice keeps mystery tied to evidence? Before opening statements, the consultant must choose whether the timeline gap will guide jurors to evidence or merely create suspense.
choices: Ask a dramatic question that the record never answers.
Show all timestamps at once and hope jurors spot the gap.
Withhold one timestamp until jurors mark the gap, then reveal the evidence card.
questions.explanation: The empty slot creates attention and the evidence card closes it. An unanswered dramatic question is unfair, and showing everything at once may fail to hold attention on the gap.

questions.prompt: A cancellation screen uses a fake progress bar to keep users from leaving. What is the clean correction? On the account-close screen, the designer must decide how to remove the false loop while still helping users check exports.
choices: Make the progress bar more cheerful.
Move the cancel button farther down the page.
Remove the false bar and keep only a real unfinished export checkbox.
questions.explanation: The real export task is a legitimate open loop; the fake bar is a trap. Cheerful design or hidden controls still manipulate held attention.

questions.prompt: A newsletter teases “one surprising secret” but delivers a routine discount. What magnetizer failure is this? Before the newsletter subject line goes live, the editor must decide whether the promised secret is real enough to earn the click.
choices: The subject line is too short to hold attention.
The loop opens curiosity that the message cannot honestly close.
The discount is not self-relevant to anyone.
questions.explanation: Curiosity is being borrowed without a matching answer. Length is not the issue, and a discount may be relevant, but it does not close the promised secret.

questions.prompt: A dentist wants parents to read a follow-up plan. Which opener is most self-relevant without being fake? At the pediatric follow-up desk, the dentist must choose an opening that names the parent’s child and next visit without pretending intimacy.
choices: “Important information for all families.”
“Your child’s left molar needs this two-week cleaning check.”
“You will regret missing this.”
questions.explanation: The specific molar makes the plan personally relevant to that family. The generic opener does not magnetize, and regret language uses pressure rather than relevance.

questions.prompt: A team loves mysteries in presentations and hides key facts in every deck. What should you tell them? In a slide review before a client meeting, the team must decide when mystery helps and when it hides facts people need.
choices: Mystery is always better than direct explanation.
Mystery should replace data when people are bored.
Mystery works only when the hidden fact is evidence the audience needs and can receive soon.
questions.explanation: Mystery should hold attention for a real answer. Treating it as a universal style turns the cue into delay, and hiding data weakens judgment.

reviewCards.front: What three cue types can hold attention rather than merely seize it?
reviewCards.back: Self-relevance, unfinished information, and mystery. Each holds attention by opening a loop the next message can legitimately close.

reviewCards.front: A blank intake field keeps volunteers watching a carrier. What is the retrieval point?
reviewCards.back: Unfinished information holds attention when the missing piece has a consequence. The blank field matters because treatment depends on it.
When the answer is delayed, irrelevant, or absent. A fair mystery asks a question the evidence can actually close.

reviewCards.front: Why is a street name stronger than generic personalization?
reviewCards.back: The street name is self-relevant only if the flood-zone change truly affects that address. The link is what holds attention.

reviewCards.front: A cancellation screen has one real export task and one fake progress bar. Which can stay?
reviewCards.back: The export task can stay because leaving has a real data consequence. The fake progress bar must go because it traps attention with false unfinished work.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is opening a loop that deserves to stay open. You use self-relevance, unfinished information, or mystery only when your next message can close the loop honestly.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a policy change affects a specific address, then name the address before showing the option table.
If learners tune out a protocol, then ask them to predict the missing consequence before revealing the note.
If a timeline gap matters, then let people mark the gap before revealing the timestamp that closes it.
If users are leaving, then show only real unfinished tasks, never fake progress.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one message people ignore. Rewrite the opener as one unanswered question that is personal, unfinished, or mysterious, then make sure the message actually answers it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, audit one open loop you created. Write the question, the promised answer, and whether the answer arrived quickly enough to justify the attention you held.

memorableLines.why: It captures why personal relevance holds attention without extra noise.

memorableLines.text: The strongest magnetizers do not yell.
memorableLines.why: It distinguishes holding attention from loud attraction.

memorableLines.text: Leave people with a question only when you are prepared to answer it.
memorableLines.why: It gives the ethical rule for mystery and open loops.
